los.text: Describe the mechanisms of inflammatory joint disease and associated pathology (rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis)
los.html:
OA
  • "joint failure".
  • Mechanical stress + ageing + genetics + low-grade inflammation
  • → chondrocyte imbalance (catabolic > anabolic; IL-1, TNF-α, MMP-13, ADAMTS-5)
  • → proteoglycan loss
  • → fibrillation
  • → cartilage loss
  • → eburnation.
  • Bone: subchondral sclerosis, cysts, osteophytes (endochondral ossification at margins).
  • Synovitis, capsule thickening, muscle weakness.
RA
  • Autoimmune.
  • Genetics (HLA-DRB1 "shared epitope") + smoking → citrullinated proteins → anti-CCP antibodies
  • RF.
  • Synovitis: synovial hyperplasia, angiogenesis, T cells, B cells/plasma cells, macrophages → TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1 → pannus (inflamed synovium) invades cartilage and bone
  • RANKL → osteoclasts → periarticular erosions and osteopenia.
  • Tendon rupture, ligament laxity → deformities (ulnar deviation, swan neck, boutonnière, Z-thumb).
Systemic RARheumatoid nodules (fibrinoid necrosis with palisading histiocytes), lung fibrosis, vasculitis, anaemia of chronic disease, ↑ CVD, scleritis, Felty's.

los.text: Describe the investigations and principles of treatment / management of rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis
sessions: Clin 3: Investigations and management of osteoarthritis
los.html:
Osteoarthritis

Clinical diagnosis(NICE)
  • ≥45, activity-related pain, no morning stiffness or stiffness ≤30 min.
  • X-ray only if atypical: LOSS (Loss of joint space, Osteophytes, Subchondral sclerosis, Subchondral cysts).
CoreEducation, exercise (strengthening + aerobic), weight loss if overweight.
Drugs
  • Topical NSAIDs first (knee/hand) → oral NSAID + PPI (lowest dose, shortest time)
  • Paracetamol and weak opioids are not routinely recommended (NICE 2022).
  • Intra-articular steroid injection for flares (short-term).
AidsWalking stick (contralateral hand), insoles, braces. Joint replacement if quality of life substantially affected.

Rheumatoid arthritis

  • Ix: RF (~70%, not specific)
    • anti-CCP (highly specific, predicts erosions)
    • CRP/ESR
    • FBC
    • X-ray hands/feet (periarticular osteopenia, erosions, uniform joint space loss)
    • USS (synovitis).
    • Monitor with DAS28.
  • Urgent rheumatology referral for suspected synovitis (treat within window of opportunity).
  • Treatment: csDMARD first: methotrexate (weekly + folic acid; monitor FBC/LFT; teratogenic, pneumonitis) ± sulfasalazine, leflunomide, hydroxychloroquine.
    • Bridging steroids for flares.
    • If inadequate response: biologics (anti-TNF: adalimumab, etanercept; rituximab; tocilizumab; abatacept) or JAK inhibitors.
    • Screen for TB/hepatitis before biologics.
  • MDT: physio, OT, podiatry; manage CV risk; vaccines.

los.text: Explain the basic biomedical principles of human gait and locomotion (eg. Mobility and stability of joints, neural pathways and stretch reflexes)
los.html:
Gait cycle
  • Stance phase (~60%): heel strike → foot flat → midstance → heel off → toe off
  • Swing phase (~40%): acceleration → midswing → deceleration.
  • Double support twice per cycle (absent in running).
Key muscles
  • Hip abductors (gluteus medius/minimus) stabilise the pelvis in single-leg stance
  • Quadriceps control knee at heel strike
  • Tibialis anterior lifts the foot in swing (prevents foot drop)
  • Gastrocnemius/soleus push off.
Joint stability
  • Bony congruity (hip ball and socket), ligaments, capsule, menisci, dynamic muscle control, proprioception.
  • Mobility vs stability trade-off (shoulder very mobile, hip very stable).
Neural control
  • Central pattern generators in spinal cord
  • Descending motor tracts
  • Cerebellum (coordination)
  • Basal ganglia
  • Vestibular and visual input
  • Proprioception (muscle spindles, Golgi tendon organs, joint receptors).
Stretch reflex
  • Muscle stretch
  • → spindle (Ia afferent)
  • → monosynaptic excitation of α motor neuron
  • → contraction (knee jerk L3–4) + reciprocal inhibition of antagonist.
  • Golgi tendon organ (Ib) → inhibits contraction under high tension.
Abnormal gaitCause
AntalgicPain: short stance on painful side
TrendelenburgWeak hip abductors (superior gluteal nerve, hip OA/DDH): pelvis drops on opposite side
High-steppingFoot drop (common peroneal nerve, L5)
Spastic/scissoringUMN lesion (stroke, CP)
Shuffling, festinantParkinson's
Broad-based ataxicCerebellar
WaddlingProximal myopathy, bilateral hip weakness

los.text: Describe the physiological and pathological cellular adaptations to injury
los.html:
Physiological adaptations
  • Responses to changed demand that are reversible.
  • Hypertrophy: ↑ cell size (non-dividing cells): skeletal muscle with exercise, LV in hypertension (pathological), uterus in pregnancy.
  • Hyperplasia: ↑ cell number (dividing cells): endometrium (oestrogen), breast in puberty/pregnancy, BPH, compensatory liver regeneration. Pathological hyperplasia may predispose to cancer (endometrial).
  • Atrophy: ↓ size/number: disuse, denervation, ↓ blood supply, poor nutrition, loss of hormonal stimulation, ageing (brain), pressure. Via ubiquitin–proteasome and autophagy.
  • Metaplasia: one mature cell type replaced by another better suited to stress; reversible but may progress to dysplasia: Barrett's oesophagus (squamous → columnar), smoker's bronchus (columnar → squamous), cervical transformation zone, bladder (schistosomiasis).
DysplasiaDisordered growth (↑ N:C ratio, pleomorphism, loss of maturation); pre-neoplastic; not an adaptation.
Cell injury when adaptation failsReversible (cell swelling, fatty change) → irreversible: necrosis (coagulative: infarcts; liquefactive: brain, abscess; caseous: TB; fat: pancreatitis; fibrinoid: vasculitis) vs apoptosis (programmed, no inflammation).
Causes of injuryHypoxia (commonest), toxins, infection, immune, physical, nutritional, genetic.
